q: Which pairing correctly matches an SSAE engagement type with the form of the practitioner's report?
choices: Agreed-upon procedures: an opinion based on reasonable assurance
Review: an opinion based on limited assurance
Examination: an opinion based on reasonable assurance
Review: a description of procedures and findings with no assurance
exp: An examination provides reasonable assurance expressed as an opinion, a review provides limited assurance expressed as a conclusion, and an agreed-upon procedures engagement reports procedures and findings without assurance. A review does not result in an opinion.

q: In a review engagement under AT-C 210, the practitioner's procedures consist primarily of which of the following?
choices: Inquiry and analytical procedures
Tests of controls and confirmation
Inspection of documents and observation
Procedures specified by the engaging party
exp: A review provides limited assurance and is performed primarily through inquiries and analytical procedures. Tests of controls and confirmations are typical of examinations, and procedures specified by the engaging party describe agreed-upon procedures.

q: A prospective client asks a CPA to examine its claims about a new product's energy efficiency. Which of the following is not a precondition for accepting the attestation engagement?
choices: The subject matter is appropriate
The criteria are suitable and will be available to intended users
The responsible party takes responsibility for the subject matter
The practitioner has previously performed attestation work for the entity
exp: AT-C 105 preconditions include that the responsible party takes responsibility for the subject matter, the subject matter is appropriate, the criteria are suitable and available to users, and the practitioner expects to obtain the needed evidence. Prior work for the entity is not a precondition.

q: Which is not one of the characteristics of suitable criteria under the attestation standards?
choices: Relevance
Measurability
Confidentiality
Objectivity
exp: Suitable criteria are relevant, objective, measurable and complete. Confidentiality is not a characteristic of suitable criteria; in fact, criteria must be available to intended users.

q: Criteria for an examination were developed by a client and a single lender and are available only to them. How does this affect the practitioner's report?
choices: The report must include an alert restricting its use to the client and the lender
The practitioner must decline the engagement
The report may be issued for general use with an emphasis paragraph
The practitioner must express a qualified opinion
exp: When criteria are available only to specified parties, the report should include an alert that restricts its use to those parties. The criteria can still be suitable, so declining or qualifying the opinion is not required.

q: A CPA is asked to perform an agreed-upon procedures engagement. Which statement about independence is correct?
choices: Independence is not required because no assurance is provided
Independence is required only if the report is for general use
Independence may be waived by the engaging party in writing
Independence is required because an agreed-upon procedures engagement is an attestation engagement
exp: All attestation engagements under the SSAEs, including agreed-upon procedures, require independence. The lack of assurance and the intended users do not change that requirement, and it cannot be waived by the client.

q: Which statement of a finding is appropriate in an agreed-upon procedures report?
choices: Nothing came to our attention that caused us to believe the invoices were not properly approved
We compared the dates on the 25 selected invoices with the shipping log and found no exceptions
Based on our review, the invoices appear to be properly supported
In our opinion, the invoices are fairly stated in all material respects
exp: Agreed-upon procedures findings are reported in clear, factual terms describing the procedure and its results. Negative assurance, review-style language and opinions are inappropriate because no assurance is provided.

q: Under SSAE 19 (AT-C 215 as revised), which of the following is required before the practitioner issues an agreed-upon procedures report?
choices: A written assertion from the responsible party about the subject matter
Participation by all report users in developing the procedures
The engaging party's acknowledgment that the procedures performed are appropriate for the intended purpose
An examination of the subject matter performed in a prior period
exp: SSAE 19 requires the engaging party to agree to the procedures and acknowledge that they are appropriate for the intended purpose, and it removed the requirement for a written assertion. Users no longer need to participate in establishing the procedures.

q: Which procedure would be inappropriate in an agreed-upon procedures engagement?
choices: Recalculating the interest expense on the listed loans
Comparing the amounts on the schedule with the general ledger
Confirming the balances of selected loans with the lenders
Evaluating whether management's assumptions for the allowance are reasonable
exp: Agreed-upon procedures must be specific enough to produce objective findings, so procedures requiring subjective judgment, such as evaluating the reasonableness of assumptions, are not appropriate. Recalculating, comparing and confirming produce factual results.

q: In an examination, the practitioner concludes that the subject matter is materially misstated and the effects are not pervasive. Under AT-C 205, how should the practitioner word the opinion?
choices: A qualified opinion expressed directly on the subject matter rather than on the responsible party's assertion
A qualified opinion expressed on the responsible party's assertion
An adverse opinion on the assertion
An unmodified opinion with an emphasis-of-matter paragraph
exp: A material misstatement that is not pervasive calls for a qualified opinion, and when the opinion is modified, AT-C 205 requires the practitioner to report directly on the subject matter rather than on the assertion. An adverse opinion is for pervasive misstatements.

q: During an examination, the practitioner cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about a significant part of the subject matter, and the possible effects could be pervasive. What is the practitioner's most appropriate response if withdrawal is not chosen?
choices: Express a qualified opinion
Disclaim an opinion
Express an adverse opinion
Convert the engagement to a review
exp: A scope limitation with possibly pervasive effects leads to a disclaimer of opinion (or withdrawal). An adverse opinion is for misstatements actually identified, not for an inability to obtain evidence.

q: Which of the following may be performed as a review engagement under the SSAEs?
choices: A review of an entity's prospective financial statements
A review of an entity's compliance with specified requirements
A review of a service organization's description and controls for a SOC 1 report
A review of pro forma financial information
exp: AT-C 310 permits examinations and reviews of pro forma financial information. The attestation standards do not permit reviews of prospective financial information or of compliance with specified requirements, and SOC 1 reports are examinations.

q: A practitioner is engaged to review pro forma financial information. What is required regarding the historical financial statements on which the pro forma adjustments are based?
choices: They must have been audited or reviewed, and the assurance on the pro forma information cannot exceed that on the historical statements
They must have been audited by the same practitioner
They need not be audited or reviewed because the review covers only the adjustments
They must be accompanied by a compilation report
exp: AT-C 310 requires that the historical financial statements have been audited or reviewed, and the level of assurance on the pro forma information is limited to the level provided on the historical statements. Another practitioner may have audited them.

q: A client asks a CPA to examine a financial presentation showing expected results if it opens a new plant, a plan that is being considered but not yet approved. What type of prospective financial information is this, and who may use it?
choices: A financial forecast, available for general use
A financial projection, generally restricted to parties negotiating directly with the responsible party
A financial forecast, restricted to management
Pro forma financial information, available for general use
exp: A projection is based on one or more hypothetical assumptions, such as a course of action not yet adopted, and is appropriate only for limited use by parties negotiating directly with the responsible party. A forecast reflects expected conditions and may be for general use.

q: Which statement must be included in a practitioner's examination report on a financial forecast?
choices: The forecasted results will be achieved
The practitioner will update the report for events after its date
Differences between forecasted and actual results may be material and the practitioner has no responsibility to update the report
The practitioner provides limited assurance on the assumptions
exp: The report cautions that prospective results may not be achieved, because events often differ from expectations, and that the practitioner has no responsibility to update the report. An examination provides reasonable assurance, not limited assurance.

q: A user auditor needs evidence about a payroll processor's controls that are relevant to the user entity's financial reporting. Which report should the user auditor request?
choices: A SOC 2 report on security and availability
A SOC 1 report on controls relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting
A SOC 3 report for general use
An agreed-upon procedures report on the processor's revenue
exp: SOC 1 reports address controls at a service organization relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting. SOC 2 and SOC 3 reports address the trust services criteria, such as security and availability, rather than financial reporting.

q: How does a Type 2 SOC 1 report differ from a Type 1 report?
choices: A Type 2 report includes the service auditor's tests of the operating effectiveness of controls over a period
A Type 2 report covers only the design of controls at a point in time
A Type 2 report is a review rather than an examination
A Type 2 report is intended for general use
exp: A Type 1 report covers the fairness of the description and the suitability of design as of a date, while a Type 2 report adds operating effectiveness throughout a specified period, with the tests and results described. Both are examinations with restricted use.

q: A service organization uses a subservice organization for data center hosting. The description excludes the subservice organization's control objectives and controls but identifies the types of controls expected at the subservice organization. Which method is being used?
choices: The inclusive method
The direct method
The carve-out method
The integrated method
exp: Under the carve-out method, the subservice organization's controls are excluded from the description and the scope of the service auditor's work, though complementary subservice organization controls are identified. The inclusive method would include those controls in the description and testing.

q: A SOC 1 report states that certain control objectives can be achieved only if user entities design and operate specified controls. What are these controls called?
choices: Compensating controls
Entity-level controls
Subservice organization controls
Complementary user entity controls
exp: Complementary user entity controls are controls the service organization assumes user entities will have in place, and user auditors need to evaluate whether their client has them. Subservice organization controls relate to a vendor of the service organization.

q: A lender engages a practitioner to examine a borrower's compliance with loan covenants. The borrower's management is responsible for compliance. In this engagement, which party is the responsible party?
choices: The borrower
The lender
The practitioner
Both the lender and the borrower jointly
exp: The responsible party is responsible for the subject matter, here the borrower's compliance; the lender is the engaging party. The practitioner obtains written representations from the responsible party, even though another party engaged the practitioner.

q: Which phrase is consistent with the conclusion in a practitioner's review report under AT-C 210?
choices: In our opinion, the schedule is presented in accordance with the criteria, in all material respects
We are not aware of any material modifications that should be made to the schedule in order for it to be in accordance with the criteria
We found no exceptions as a result of the procedures performed
The schedule is presented fairly because management has asserted so
exp: A review provides limited assurance, expressed as a conclusion that the practitioner is not aware of material modifications needed. An opinion is reserved for examinations, and factual findings are the format for agreed-upon procedures.

q: A practitioner engaged to perform an examination is asked by the client, before the report is issued, to change the engagement to agreed-upon procedures. Which circumstance is most likely to be a reasonable justification for the change?
choices: The practitioner has found evidence that the subject matter is materially misstated
The client refuses to provide access to key records
A change in the user's requirements means an examination is no longer needed
The client wants to avoid a qualified opinion
exp: A change in circumstances affecting users' needs is generally a reasonable justification for changing to a lower level of service. A request driven by restricted access or an expected modified opinion is not, because it would avoid reporting a problem.

q: Under SSAE 21, what distinguishes a direct examination engagement from an assertion-based examination?
choices: In a direct engagement, the practitioner provides only limited assurance
In a direct engagement, the responsible party does not take responsibility for the subject matter
In a direct engagement, the report is always restricted to management
In a direct engagement, the practitioner measures or evaluates the underlying subject matter against the criteria
exp: In a direct examination (AT-C 206), the practitioner measures or evaluates the subject matter against the criteria and reports an opinion with reasonable assurance; the responsible party still takes responsibility for the subject matter. In an assertion-based engagement, the responsible party performs the measurement.

q: When determining materiality for an examination of a company's greenhouse gas emissions statement, which consideration is most appropriate?
choices: Use 5% of the entity's pretax income
Consider both quantitative and qualitative factors in light of the information needs of the intended users
Use the same materiality as in the company's financial statement audit
Materiality is not relevant because the subject matter is nonfinancial
exp: Attestation materiality is judged relative to intended users and the subject matter, considering both quantitative and qualitative factors. Financial-statement benchmarks do not apply to nonfinancial measures such as tons of emissions.

q: In an examination of an entity's compliance with specified requirements under AT-C 315, the practitioner identifies material noncompliance with one requirement that is not pervasive. What should the practitioner's report contain?
choices: A qualified opinion on compliance
An unmodified opinion with the noncompliance described in a separate paragraph
A disclaimer of opinion
A review conclusion on compliance
exp: Material noncompliance that is not pervasive results in a qualified opinion; pervasive noncompliance results in an adverse opinion. An unmodified opinion is inappropriate when material noncompliance exists.

q: In an attestation examination, through what date should the practitioner inquire about subsequent events that could affect the subject matter?
choices: The end of the period covered by the subject matter
The date the engagement letter was signed
The date of the practitioner's report
The date the report is distributed to users
exp: The practitioner considers events up to the date of the report that could require adjustment or disclosure. Stopping at period end would miss events that occur during fieldwork, and the practitioner has no duty to search after the report date.

q: A practitioner examining an entity's emissions data uses an environmental engineer as a specialist. Which statement is correct?
choices: The practitioner may reduce responsibility for the opinion by naming the specialist in the report
The practitioner need not evaluate the specialist's work if the specialist is certified
Use of a specialist is prohibited in attestation engagements
The practitioner should evaluate the specialist's competence, capabilities and objectivity and the adequacy of the specialist's work
exp: AT-C 205 allows practitioners to use specialists but requires evaluating their competence, capabilities and objectivity and whether their work is adequate for the practitioner's purposes. Naming the specialist does not reduce the practitioner's responsibility.

q: From whom does the practitioner request written representations in an attestation examination, and as of what date?
choices: From the responsible party, dated as of the date of the practitioner's report
From the engaging party only, dated as of the end of the subject matter period
From the intended users, dated as of the engagement acceptance date
From the practitioner's own engagement team, dated as of report release
exp: Written representations are requested from the responsible party and should be dated as of the report date, covering all periods addressed by the report. The engaging party may also be asked when it differs from the responsible party, but the responsible party is the key source.

q: Under SSAE 19, which statement about the procedures in an agreed-upon procedures engagement is correct?
choices: The procedures must be fixed in the engagement letter and can never change
The procedures may be developed or modified during the engagement, as long as the engaging party agrees and acknowledges their appropriateness before the report is issued
The practitioner may add procedures to provide negative assurance
The procedures must include tests of internal control
exp: SSAE 19 allows procedures to be refined during the engagement, provided the engaging party agrees to them and acknowledges that they are appropriate for the intended purpose before the report is released. Negative assurance is never provided in agreed-upon procedures.

q: A practitioner is asked to provide assurance about a nonprofit's sustainability report, and the board wants a lower-cost engagement than an examination but still wants some assurance. Which engagement best meets this request?
choices: An agreed-upon procedures engagement
A compilation engagement
A review engagement
An audit under GAAS
exp: A review provides limited assurance at a lower cost than an examination. Agreed-upon procedures and compilations provide no assurance, and an audit under GAAS applies to historical financial statements, not a sustainability report.
